title: Electromagnetic Spectrum

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Electromagnetic Waves

summary: Electromagnetic waves span an enormous range of wavelengths/frequencies (radio waves to gamma rays), all travelling at the same speed c in vacuum, differing only in wavelength/frequency and hence in how they interact with matter and in their practical applications.
explanation: An electromagnetic (EM) wave consists of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (a TRANSVERSE wave), requiring NO medium to travel (unlike sound) and travelling through vacuum at the constant speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s, predicted directly by Maxwell's equations. The EM spectrum, in order of INCREASING frequency (decreasing wavelength): radio waves (longest wavelength, used in communication/broadcasting), microwaves (radar, microwave ovens, mobile communication), infrared (heating effects, thermal imaging, remote controls), visible light (the only range directly detectable by the human eye), ultraviolet (causes tanning/sunburn, used for sterilisation, absorbed largely by the ozone layer), X-rays (medical imaging, high penetrating power), and gamma rays (highest frequency/energy, emitted by radioactive nuclei, most penetrating and most dangerous to biological tissue). All EM waves travel at the SAME speed c in vacuum regardless of frequency/wavelength (v = fλ = c for all of them in vacuum), but they interact very differently with matter — higher frequency (hence higher photon energy, E = hf) generally means greater penetrating power and greater potential for biological/ionising damage, which is why gamma rays and X-rays require careful shielding while radio waves are harmless at ordinary intensities. Different regions of the spectrum are produced by different physical processes: radio waves from oscillating currents in an antenna/circuit, infrared from vibrating molecules/warm bodies, visible/UV light from atomic electronic transitions, X-rays from high-energy electron transitions or deceleration of fast electrons, and gamma rays from nuclear transitions/radioactive decay.
commonMisconceptions: Assuming EM waves need a medium to travel, like sound does — EM waves are unique in requiring NO medium at all; they travel through vacuum, which is exactly how sunlight reaches Earth through space.

Believing higher-wavelength (lower-frequency) EM waves like radio waves are somehow 'weaker' versions of visible light — different regions of the spectrum aren't weaker/stronger versions of each other, they are produced by entirely different physical mechanisms and interact with matter completely differently.

Assuming visible light is the most energetic or most complete part of the spectrum simply because it's what we can see — visible light is actually just a very narrow slice of the full EM spectrum, sandwiched between infrared and ultraviolet, with far more energetic (X-ray, gamma) and far less energetic (radio, microwave) regions extending well beyond it.
examples: A television remote control uses infrared waves to send signals, while a mobile phone uses microwaves for communication with a nearby cell tower.
X-rays are used in medical imaging because their high penetrating power lets them pass through soft tissue but be absorbed more by denser bone, creating a contrast image.
genZNote: Radio waves and gamma rays are cousins — same wave family, wildly different energy levels.
